summary: Preregistered online RCT with N=704 UK Prolific adults across five arms. Participants practised fraction arithmetic with a GPT-OSS-120B tutor that gives complete answers only on explicit request, then took a six-item unaided test. LLM-generated metacognitive feedback after each item (how you used the assistant, what it meant for your practice, a monitoring cue) lowered answer offloading (OR 0.47, CI 0.22-1.00) and raised unaided accuracy (OR 1.51, CI 0.98-2.33; preregistered one-sided p=.03). An effort-based points reward changed neither outcome. Access to the assistant did not lower unaided performance versus a no-AI control, so no deskilling effect appeared in this design.

claims.claim: Metacognitive feedback reduces answer offloading to the LLM
claims.evidence: Table 3 H2a: OR 0.47 [0.22,1.00], one-sided p=.026, 5,022 item observations from 558 participants. Appendix H participant-level difference: -5.05 pp [-8.97,-1.14]. Descriptive offloading: 0.13/0.10 with feedback vs 0.18/0.15 without.

claims.claim: Metacognitive feedback improves subsequent unaided test performance
claims.evidence: H2b: OR 1.51 [0.98,2.33], one-sided p=.030. Participant-level difference +5.28 pp [-0.14,10.70]. In both analyses the two-sided CI includes no effect. Feedback arm 0.67 vs AI-only 0.62 vs no-AI 0.65, so it restores the no-AI level rather than exceeding it (authors concede in §6.3). The test is six items taken immediately after practice.

claims.claim: An effort-based reward did not reduce offloading or improve performance
claims.evidence: H3a OR 0.66 [0.31,1.40], p=.139; H3b OR 0.76 [0.50,1.18]. Participant-level H3a p=.0501. The reward cut any AI use (OR 0.39 [0.23,0.66]) but not the share of complete-answer requests.

claims.claim: The interventions protect against deskilling (title and framing)
claims.evidence: H1 not supported: the AI-only arm did not perform worse than no-AI (OR 0.80 [0.42,1.51], p=.244). No deskilling effect was demonstrated, so 'designing against deskilling' was not tested. There is no delayed test (acknowledged in §6.5).

claims.claim: Answer offloading is associated with lower unaided performance
claims.evidence: Exploratory: +10 pp offloading corresponds to OR 0.68 [0.62,0.74]. Correlational; prior ability is a plausible confound, as the authors note.

patterns.note: Out of domain. Feedback on how much work the learner delegated, compared against the same assistant without feedback (a reasonable alternative), wins on both preregistered one-sided outcomes. Effects are small (about 5 pp), the two-sided CI for test score includes zero, the test is immediate, and the task is fraction arithmetic with general-population adults, not developers or code.

An LLM classifier (GPT-OSS-120B plus a numeric rule check) labels assistance level for the reward. It agreed with intended labels on 198 held-out synthetic dialogues; no human-labelled real dialogues were reported.

methodology.sample: N=704 (720 recruited; 5 incomplete, 11 failed the honesty check), UK Prolific adults aged 18-80, five arms of 137-146. 10 learning items (9 measured) and 6 unaided test items, generated from templates.
methodology.baselines: No-AI control and AI-only (same request-gated assistant without interventions); 2x2 factorial for feedback x reward
methodology.models: GPT-OSS-120B via Amazon Bedrock (assistant and classifier at temperature 0; feedback generator at temperature 0.7)
methodology.variance: Item-level mixed-effects logistic regression with participant random intercepts; two-sided 95% CIs; preregistered one-sided tests; participant-level t-test/ANOVA robustness checks
methodology.ablations: Feedback and reward separated by the 2x2 design. The three feedback components are not separated (acknowledged).

standards.peer_review: Not stated (repository named for CHI 2027 submission)
standards.artifacts: Analysis code, anonymized data and LLM reporting in an anonymous 4open.science repository. System, classifier and feedback prompts in appendices.
standards.preregistration: AsPredicted (hypotheses, design, sample size, exclusions, analysis plan)

biases.detail: Fraction arithmetic with template items and a six-item immediate test. No programming, codebase or developer population.
The title claims design against deskilling, but the study found no deskilling from AI access (H1 null).
An immediate post-practice test measures short-term transfer, not durable skill. The paper's design recommendations generalize well beyond what was measured.
One LLM (GPT-OSS-120B) for assistant, feedback and classifier.
UK, English-first-language Prolific workers with at least 99% approval; not developers.

coi.affiliations: LMU Munich; Munich Center for Machine Learning
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: None (open-weight model used as a component)

verdict_reason: Off-topic under the KB scope. This is a well-run, preregistered, adequately powered RCT, but it studies fraction-arithmetic practice by general-population adults, not software development with LLMs or developers using them. The mechanism it tests (feedback on how much work you delegated, with complete answers available only on request) is relevant to P41 as a hypothesis to test with developers, not as evidence about them. Even in its own domain, the 'deskilling' framing is unbacked (H1 null) and the test-score gain's two-sided CI includes zero.
applicability: Does not transfer as evidence. As a design hypothesis for a developer learning mode in the onboarding harness: after an agent completes a change for a developer new to the ingestion domain, show a short mirror of what the agent decided versus what the developer did, and make 'give me the full solution' an explicit choice rather than the default. Points-style incentives for using less AI are not worth building, since they cut usage without changing how it was used. Before adopting either, the team would need its own measure, such as the developer explaining or modifying the change unaided a week later.

conflicts_with.detail: There, an Aider agent that edits code by default lowered CS students' comprehension of their own code. Here, AI access did not lower unaided performance when complete answers required an explicit request. The authors attribute this to request friction; the difference in defaults across the two studies is untested.
